## Tap a tune on one note and see what survives

Plenty of familiar tunes stay recognisable when you tap them out on a single
pitch. When that happens, rhythm is carrying more of the identity than the note
names are. Flatten the durations instead, giving every note the same length, and
a different part of the tune comes through in its rise and fall. An ordinary
melody hands you both streams fused together, so listening to the finished line
won't tell you which one did the work.

*Contour* is a deliberately coarse description of pitch motion: up, down, or
unchanged. It forgets interval size and it forgets register. Rhythm splits into
onsets and durations. Once those streams live in separate arrays, you can run
the comparison cleanly: flatten the pitches and keep the timing, keep the shape
and replace the timing, or shrink every interval without touching a single
direction.

## One phrase, four reductions

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 104
use_synth :pluck

notes = [64, 64, 66, 64, 69, 68, 64, 64, 66, 64, 71, 69]
durations = [0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 2, 0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 2]

define :play_phrase do |notes, durations|
  notes.zip(durations).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.75
    sleep duration
  end
end

define :contour do |notes|
  notes.each_cons(2).map do |a, b|
    b > a ? :up : (b < a ? :down : :same)
  end
end

shape = contour(notes)
contour_notes = [60]
shape.each do |direction|
  step = {up: 2, down: -2, same: 0}[direction]
  contour_notes << contour_notes[-1] + step
end

play_phrase notes, durations
sleep 2
play_phrase Array.new(notes.length, 64), durations
sleep 2
play_phrase contour_notes, Array.new(notes.length, 0.75)
sleep 2
play_phrase contour_notes, durations
```

Pass one gives you the whole phrase. Pass two keeps the rhythm and deletes every
pitch change, so whatever identity is left belongs to timing. Pass three rebuilds
the bare contour on equal durations. Pass four hands that rebuilt shape back its
original rhythm. Which of the middle two do you recognise faster? Answer before
you reach the explanation, because the answer varies by tune and by listener,
and your first reaction is the useful data point.

## Break one stream at a time

1. Replace every duration with `1`. The pitches are untouched and their long and
   short values vanish. Notice which fragments still hang together, and where
   the phrase loses a boundary it used to have.

2. Change the rebuilt contour step from two semitones to one. Every direction
   holds and the line contracts into half its former range. That's a direct test
   of how much interval size was contributing beyond the bare signs.

3. Reverse `durations` only. Notes keep their order and the long values now land
   on different pitches. Listen for a new grouping; you won't hear a backwards
   version of the tune, because only one of the two streams was reversed.

## What each reduction throws away

`zip` aligns the two streams by index, and `play_phrase` combines them only at
playback. A timing experiment therefore never touches pitch data, and a pitch
transformation leaves the rhythm alone. Because the code change stays local, the
listening comparison stays local too.

Contour is lossy on purpose. Many quite different melodies collapse onto the
same string of directions, which is what makes family resemblance visible and
reconstruction impossible. A duration list is incomplete in its own way once
meter, accent and articulation get involved. So the program asks a narrower
question, one you can actually answer: given these reductions of this phrase,
which surviving feature carries more of what you recognise?

Rhythm often turns out to carry a startling amount, and that finding belongs in
a listening log rather than in a rule. Test it on another person before you
promote it. The uncertainty pays off later in transcription work, where a secure
rhythmic outline with approximate pitches will often get you to the phrase
faster than exact pitches floating at uncertain times.

You can enrich contour in stages. Split `:up` into `:step_up` and `:leap_up`, or
store the full signed semitone difference and stop reducing altogether. Each
added distinction keeps more identity and lets fewer source melodies share an
encoding. Use the coarsest representation that answers the question in front of
you, then add detail the moment two cases you care about collapse together.

## Run the test on somebody else

Choose a familiar tune of eight to sixteen notes and build three anonymous
versions of it: its original rhythm on one repeated pitch, its contour on equal
durations, and its original rhythm paired with the contour rebuilt in whole
tones. Play them for a willing listener and record which version they name
first.

Hold synth, tempo, register and amplitude fixed across all three, and keep the
exact arrays next to the observation you write down. That record makes your
result reproducible without pretending that one listener has settled the general
question. [Lesson 33](33-motive-sequence-development.qmd) takes the opposite approach and keeps a short idea intact
while changing everything around it.
